narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 61.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were your academic performance in the third year of law school, your LSAT score, and your first-year academic performance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. Standing in the third decile is noticeably lower than the average of accepted students (around the sixth decile), signaling that your later-year grades were weaker than most who were admitted. Your first-year ranking also worked against you, again placing you in the third decile compared with an average of sixth among accepted applicants. These two academic signals together created a clear pattern of below-average performance that the model found concerning.

Your LSAT score of 36 worked in the opposite direction. It is only slightly below the accepted average of 37.2, so it modestly pulled the prediction back toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the academic-ranking concerns.

Your family income, undergraduate GPA, full-time status, gender, and race played little or no role; the decision rested almost entirely on the three academic factors above.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses or enroll elsewhere, and consider retaking the LSAT to raise that score. These steps would directly address the features that most influenced the current outcome. (218 words)
